title: The Thyroid Gland: What It Does and How It Can Go Wrong
content:
The thyroid is a small, butterfly-shaped gland at the front of the neck, just below the Adam's apple. Despite its size, it has an outsized influence on the body: it produces hormones — mainly thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) — that regulate metabolism, essentially controlling how quickly cells convert nutrients into energy. Thyroid hormones affect heart rate, body temperature, digestion, energy levels, mood, and even skin and hair, which is why thyroid dysfunction can produce such a wide, seemingly unrelated range of symptoms.

The thyroid itself is regulated by a feedback loop involving the pituitary gland, a small structure at the base of the brain. The pituitary releases thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), which signals the thyroid to produce more T4 and T3. When thyroid hormone levels are adequate, the pituitary reduces TSH output; when levels are low, it increases TSH to prompt more production. This is why TSH is usually the first blood test used to screen thyroid function — it tends to change even before T4 and T3 levels move outside their own reference ranges, making it a sensitive early indicator.

When the thyroid produces too little hormone, the condition is called hypothyroidism, or an underactive thyroid. The body's processes slow down: common symptoms include fatigue and low energy, unexplained weight gain, feeling unusually cold, dry skin, constipation, depressed mood, memory or concentration difficulties, muscle aches, and menstrual cycle changes. In many parts of the world, the most common cause of hypothyroidism is an autoimmune condition called Hashimoto's thyroiditis, in which the immune system gradually attacks the thyroid gland.

When the thyroid produces too much hormone, the condition is called hyperthyroidism, or an overactive thyroid. This speeds the body's processes up: common symptoms include unintended weight loss despite normal or increased appetite, a rapid or irregular heartbeat, nervousness or irritability, tremor, heat intolerance and excessive sweating, and sometimes visible eye changes. Graves' disease, another autoimmune condition, is the most common cause.

Both conditions can develop gradually, and in mild or early cases, symptoms may be subtle enough to be mistaken for stress, poor sleep, or simply "getting older" — which is part of why thyroid testing is a common and reasonable step when someone reports persistent, hard-to-explain fatigue, mood changes, or weight changes, even without other obvious thyroid symptoms.

Thyroid conditions are also notably more common in women than men, and can be particularly relevant around pregnancy and menopause, since thyroid function and reproductive hormones interact. Thyroid disorders are additionally a recognized, treatable cause of menstrual irregularity, which is why thyroid testing often appears alongside other hormone testing when irregular cycles are being evaluated.

The good news is that both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism are generally very manageable once diagnosed. Hypothyroidism is typically treated with a daily synthetic thyroid hormone replacement (levothyroxine), which restores normal hormone levels and reverses symptoms over time. Hyperthyroidism has several treatment paths depending on the cause and severity, including medications that reduce hormone production, radioactive iodine treatment, or, less commonly, surgery. This is general educational information, not a diagnosis — an abnormal TSH or thyroid hormone level on a report is a starting point for a clinician to investigate further, not a conclusion in itself.
